questions.question: Which hash property is most directly used by Lamport OTS security?
options: Preimage resistance (one-wayness)
Reversible encoding (invertibility)
Output expansion (longer output)
Compression ratio (short output)
questions.explanation: Verification checks hashes of revealed secrets, so forging requires inverting the hash on at least one commitment.

questions.question: How many bits are in a SHA-256 digest?
options: 128 bits total
160 bits total
256 bits total
512 bits total
questions.explanation: SHA-256 outputs 32 bytes, which is 256 bits.

questions.question: In Lamport OTS, what does the public key contain for each bit position i?
options: Two hashed commitments H(sk0[i]) and H(sk1[i])
Two plaintext secrets sk0[i] and sk1[i] for signing
One hash of the message digest bit d[i] for reuse
One RSA modulus shared across all bit positions
questions.explanation: The public key publishes hashes of both possible secrets; the private key keeps the secrets themselves.

questions.question: A Lamport signature on SHA256(message) contains which data?
options: All 512 private secrets for every bit position
Exactly 256 revealed secrets chosen by digest bits
Exactly 256 hashes of secrets to keep them hidden
A single 64-byte value that replaces all secrets
questions.explanation: For each digest bit, the signer reveals one of the two secrets at that position.

questions.question: If two implementations disagree on MSB-first vs LSB-first bit order, what is the most likely outcome?
options: Valid signatures fail verification across implementations
Signatures become smaller because fewer bits are used
Security increases because the digest bits are permuted
Public keys shrink because only one key half is needed
questions.explanation: The verifier must select the same per-bit commitments the signer used; a bit-order mismatch selects different secrets.

questions.question: What is the main cryptographic risk of signing two different messages with the same Lamport key?
options: Many positions reveal both secrets sk0[i] and sk1[i]
The hash function stops being deterministic for digests
The verifier can no longer compute SHA-256 correctly
Signatures get shorter and lose their fixed-length form
questions.explanation: Once both secrets for a position are exposed, an attacker can satisfy either digest bit at that position in a forgery.

questions.question: In the lesson leakage check, what does a 'fully revealed position' mean?
options: Both sk0[i] and sk1[i] have been exposed via signatures
The digest bit at i is always 1 for every signed message
The public key is missing the commitment for that index
The signature length is not equal to the digest bit length
questions.explanation: A position is fully revealed once signatures have exposed secrets for both possible digest bit values at that index.

questions.question: How do practical hash-based signature schemes get many one-time keys into a multi-use system?
options: Authenticate many OTS public keys with a Merkle tree root
Reuse the same OTS key but rotate the bit order each time
Encrypt each OTS secret under the public key for reuse
Replace the hash with RSA so the key can be reused safely
questions.explanation: Merkle-tree composition lets you commit to many one-time public keys under a single root, consuming one leaf per signature.
